title: Elections and the Regression Discontinuity Design: Lessons from Close U.S. House Races, 1942–2008
research_question: Are the winners and losers of very close U.S. House elections comparable to one another, such that bare victory can be treated as effectively random? Relatedly, how large is the causal advantage conferred on a party by narrowly winning a House seat, and through what mechanisms do candidates in tight races end up on the winning side?
data_description: The authors construct an original dataset on U.S. House of Representatives general elections covering 1942–2008, with the district-election as the unit of observation. The data substantially correct and extend the Lee (2008) dataset (originally derived from ICPSR 1995 candidate/constituency files), fixing miscoded outcomes, candidate prior office-holding, and redistricting indicators, and adding dozens of demographic, political, and candidate-level variables. Key variables include Democratic vote margin, lagged and lead Democratic victory and vote share, candidate prior House terms and political experience, campaign spending and donations (available from 1972 and 1980 respectively), Congressional Quarterly pre-election race ratings (from ~1954), partisanship of the governor and secretary of state, normal presidential vote, and district demographics. The authors also hand-collected detailed narratives, initial reported margins, and recount information for a random sample of 75 races decided by under 0.75%.
institutional_context: The setting is post-war U.S. House elections, where a single plurality threshold determines which party wins a district seat. Although bare winners and losers might appear interchangeable, House campaigns are highly professionalized contests in which incumbents and their parties typically enjoy advantages in fundraising, candidate experience, party organization, and expert handicapping (e.g., Congressional Quarterly ratings). National partisan tides systematically shape which party's seats are at risk in a given cycle, so narrow victories for each party tend to occur in years favorable to the opposing party. Very close races also trigger distinctive procedures—recounts (commonly above a 0.5% margin threshold), legal challenges, and intensified last-minute campaign mobilization, get-out-the-vote spending, and discretionary decisions by local election officials—that differentiate razor-thin contests from typical House elections. The authors use Lee's (2008) study of the incumbent party advantage as a reference application.
